title: I Remember, I Remember
tagline: The house he was born in, the garden and the lilac tree — and the dusk where the poem turns.

overview.intro: Thomas Hood’s gentle lyric — not to be confused with Wordsworth’s poem of the same title — is spoken by a man passing the house where he was born and letting memory lift him through the day. The poem moves through three remembered times: the morning of childhood, with the sun that came into his bedroom like a guest; the afternoon, with the garden, the lilac tree planted by his father, and the birds that were so near he could have touched them; and the evening, when as a boy he watched the light go down and imagined that, at last, he had reached the end of the day. The third stanza is where the poem’s tenderness turns: the speaker admits that the day of his life has many hours yet, but none of them will be like those — and then comes the famous correction, that even the sun that rose on his birth never rose so bright for him as it did that day. This chapter follows the remembered scenes and the poem’s quiet movement from joy to loss.

learn.title: Before you read: memory spoken aloud

blocks.text: The poem’s opening is its method: the repetition of “I remember” is not merely a refrain but a way of speaking memory into being, each repetition lifting one more scene out of the past. Hood’s device is the apostrophe of time itself — he addresses the hours and the light as if they were present and listening — and the poem’s three stanzas behave like three turns of a head: the morning, the afternoon, the evening of childhood, each remembered at the age when it happened rather than from the adult’s distance. Notice how the detail is domestic and exact: a bedroom, a garden, a lilac tree a father planted, birds close enough to touch, a watched sunset. Nothing is grand; the whole world of the poem is one property and one family. It is worth knowing, too, that this poem is regularly confused with Wordsworth’s “I Remember, I Remember”, which is a different poem about a different childhood and a different consolation. Ours is Hood’s, and its distinguishing mark is its ending — a poem that corrects its own claim about happiness and leaves the reader with a brightness that was once, and can never be again.

items: The refrain “I remember” performs memory as it names it.
Three times of day, each held at the age it happened.
The setting is domestic and exact: house, garden, tree, birds, sunset.
Do not confuse Hood’s poem with Wordsworth’s of the same title.
The ending corrects the poem’s own claim about happiness.

blocks.text: Published readings divide the poem by the time of day each stanza remembers. Morning: the speaker remembers dawn in his bedroom, when the sunlight came in through the window and he woke to find it standing by his bed like a visiting guest — a child’s experience of light as a person, and the reason the day could only get brighter after such a beginning. Afternoon: the garden takes over — the lilac tree that his father planted, the birds that were so close he could almost have touched them from where he stood, and the general nearness of childhood, in which everything worth reaching was within reach. Evening: as a boy he watched the sun go down and believed, in the optimism of childhood, that he had come to the end of the day and its pleasures — only to learn the adult correction, that the day of a life is long and that these particular hours cannot be had again. The three scenes therefore enact a whole life compressed into a day: the brightness of beginning, the fullness of the middle, and the dusk of understanding. The movement from scene to scene is gentle — no argument, only remembering — which is why the final stanza’s shift lands with the weight it does.

learn.title: The turn: dusk, correction and the brightest sunrise

blocks.text: The poem’s close is where Hood’s lyric differs from simple nostalgia. The speaker confesses that, watching the sunset as a boy, he thought the day’s pleasures were over — and then the adult voice corrects him: there are many hours left in this day, the day of his life, but none of them will be like those. Published readings treat this as the poem’s pivot from memory to loss: the child believed he had reached an end that was only an evening, while the man knows he has reached a different end entirely — the end of access to those hours. And yet the poem refuses to end in grief. The final correction turns the loss into a kind of consecration: even the sun that rose on the day of his birth never rose so brightly for him as it did that morning in his childhood room. The happiness is therefore not cancelled but fixed — it happened once, absolutely, and cannot be diminished by the fact that it is over. The last effect is double: the reader feels the ache of time passing and, in the same breath, the completeness of a moment that time cannot revise. That double feeling — gratitude and loss held together — is the poem’s true subject and the thing a good answer should name.

items: The child mistook an evening for the end of the day.
The adult knows: hours remain, but none like those.
Loss is then corrected into completion — nothing dims the first brightness.
The final feeling is double: gratitude and loss at once.

blocks.text: Memory and childhood are the poem’s surface, and Hood handles them by refusing generalities: everything remembered is a particular object — window, bed, tree, bird, sunset — because memory itself works in objects. The passage of time is the second theme, and the poem compresses it into a single day so that a lifetime becomes watchable: morning ambition, afternoon fullness, evening understanding. Loss runs beneath both, but it is loss qualified by gratitude — the poem’s characteristic note. Technically, the piece relies on apostrophe (addressing the hours as “you”), on the refrain that makes remembering audible, on concrete imagery drawn from one household, and on a quiet iambic movement that supports the rocking quality of recollection. Two cautions for the examination: identify the poet as Thomas Hood, and keep the three times of day in order — sunrise, garden, sunset — because questions often ask what the evening stanza contributes, and the answer is the poem’s entire change of feeling.

learn.title: For the examination, and what to verify yourself

blocks.text: Structure questions ask for the three remembered times and what each contributes — prepare the table above in prose form. Image questions favour the sunrise, the lilac tree and the sunset; be ready to explain the personification of the morning light and the significance of a tree planted by the father. The most common long question asks about the poem’s ending: the child’s mistaken belief, the adult’s correction about the remaining hours, and the final reversal that fixes the childhood sunrise as the brightest he ever knew. Context questions sometimes test the confusion with Wordsworth — always name Thomas Hood. As everywhere on this site, the poem’s lines are not reproduced here: verify any wording you quote in an answer against your own prescribed copy, and keep the attribution exact.

questions.prompt: Which poet wrote “I Remember, I Remember” studied in this syllabus?
questions.explanation: The prescribed poem is Thomas Hood’s lyric of remembered childhood; Wordsworth wrote a different poem with the same title, and the confusion is a favourite examination trap.
questions.commonMistake: Attributing the poem to Wordsworth is the most common error on this text.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker remember from the morning of his childhood?
options: Sunlight entering his bedroom and standing at his bed like a guest
His father calling him to the garden
A carriage arriving at the door
questions.answer: Sunlight entering his bedroom and standing at his bed like a guest
questions.explanation: The morning stanza is built on the personified sunrise, a visitor that makes the day begin brighter than any that follows.
questions.commonMistake: The light is personified as a guest; nothing else comes into the room.

questions.prompt: Which image belongs to the afternoon stanza?
options: The lilac tree planted by his father
questions.answer: The lilac tree planted by his father
questions.explanation: The afternoon memory is the garden with its lilac tree and the near birds — the fullness and nearness of childhood.
questions.commonMistake: Keep the three times straight: sunrise is morning, sunset is evening.

questions.prompt: What does the final stanza of the poem do?
options: Corrects the child’s belief about the day and then fixes the childhood sunrise as the brightest he knew
Describes a walk through the garden
Compares childhood with old age in a single sentence
Predicts a happy future for the speaker
questions.answer: Corrects the child’s belief about the day and then fixes the childhood sunrise as the brightest he knew
questions.explanation: The turn is double: first the adult’s correction that hours remain but none like those, then the reversal that no sun ever rose so brightly for him.
questions.commonMistake: The ending is not merely sad; it converts loss into completion.

questions.prompt: The speaker remembers a tree planted by his ______ in the garden.
questions.explanation: The lilac tree is a family object, which is how Hood anchors memory in something the household itself made.
questions.commonMistake: It is the father’s tree, not the speaker’s own planting.

questions.prompt: What three times of day does the speaker remember, and what belongs to each?
questions.answer: Morning: the sunrise coming into his bedroom and standing at his bedside like a guest. Afternoon: the garden with the lilac tree his father planted and the birds so near he might have touched them. Evening: watching the sun go down as a boy and believing he had come to the end of the day and its pleasures.
questions.explanation: All three must appear in order with their images, because the poem’s structure is its meaning.
questions.commonMistake: Do not merge afternoon and evening; the sunset belongs to the third movement.

questions.prompt: What mistake did the boy make while watching the sunset, and how does the adult correct it?
questions.answer: The boy believed that in watching the sun go down he had come to the end of the day and of its pleasures — as if a day could end at the first dusk. The adult corrects him twice: there are many hours left in this day of his life, but none of them will be like those he remembers — and then, in the final reversal, no sunrise has ever been as bright for him as the one that entered his childhood room.
questions.explanation: The correction has two stages — the remaining hours, and the brightest sunrise — and both are needed for full marks.
questions.commonMistake: Answering only the first correction misses the poem’s final reversal.

questions.prompt: How does the poem move from memory to loss, and how does it finally resolve that loss?
questions.answer: The poem moves by degrees rather than by argument. Each stanza remembers a scene whole — morning light, the garden, the watched sunset — and each is held at the age when it happened, so that memory initially feels like possession: the speaker can go back there at will. The change comes in the third movement, when the child’s belief that the day has ended is answered by the man’s knowledge that hours remain but none like those. At that point the remembered scenes stop being retrievable and become lost, and nostalgia turns into the pang of time passing. The resolution is not philosophical but emotional: the poem’s final correction — that no sun ever rose so brightly for him as that childhood morning — refuses both consolation and complaint. The happiness is not diminished because it is over; it is fixed, absolute, and outside time’s reach to revise. The reader is therefore left holding two things at once, the ache of what cannot return and the gratitude that it occurred — and that double feeling, not sadness alone, is the poem’s answer to loss.
questions.explanation: The answer tracks the three stages — memory as possession, memory as loss, memory as completion — and names the double feeling at the end.
questions.commonMistake: Do not end the answer at “the poem is sad”; the final reversal is the resolution.

questions.prompt: Describe the images used in the poem and show what each contributes to its theme.
questions.answer: The images are small, exact and domestic, and each carries a stage of the theme. The sunrise entering the bedroom like a guest gives light a person’s courtesy, so that childhood begins as a visitation of brightness — and this image is the one the poem’s last line returns to, which is why it must be remembered precisely. The lilac tree planted by his father anchors memory in an object the family itself created: the past is not abstract but a thing growing in a particular garden. The birds near enough to touch express the nearness of childhood, in which everything worth reaching was within reach — the visual form of a time when the world was at arm’s length. And the sunset watched as a boy is the image of premature conclusion: the child reads the dusk as the day’s end, which the man knows it was not, and from this image the poem’s loss is born. Together the four images trace the theme — brightness, belonging, nearness, misreading — and the final line gathers them back into one, fixing the first sunrise as the standard against which every later day is measured.
questions.explanation: Each image is described, tied to a stage of the theme, and the answer shows how the final line gathers them.
questions.commonMistake: Listing images without saying what each contributes will not satisfy the “show” in the question.

questions.prompt: Is this poem an escape from the present or a way of facing it? Discuss.
questions.answer: It begins like an escape and ends like a facing. The refrain and the addressed hours suggest a man stepping out of the present into the past for relief, and the domestic scenes — bedroom, garden, tree — are the kind of places one retreats to because the present has worn thin. But the third stanza removes the retreat’s foundation: the child who thought the day was over was mistaken, and the man who remembers him cannot pretend that his own day shares that innocence. The poem therefore turns from recollection to accounting — hours remaining, none like those — which is a confrontation with the present rather than an escape from it. And the final correction refuses even the comfortable grief that such confrontation usually produces: instead of mourning that the brightness is gone, the speaker declares that no other sunrise equalled it, converting the past from something lost into something secured. One can argue both readings in an examination and win, provided the evidence is staged: the remembered scenes for escape, the correction of the boy’s mistake and the last line for facing. The stronger view is that the poem teaches how to hold a lost time without either denying the loss or being destroyed by it — which is why it endures as the comfort it appears to be.
questions.explanation: The answer stages both readings with specific evidence, then argues for the stronger synthesis rather than leaving the question open.
questions.commonMistake: Do not pick a side without evidence; the question rewards an argued position with staged examples.
